name: Ben Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my uncle Clive's building firm in a market town, four of us plus subcontractors. We do extensions, roofs and barn conversions for farmers and retired couples. I'm the junior, so I'm humping slates up the ladder, battening roofs, cutting rafters when Clive lets me, and keeping the yard tidy. I like being outside and I like that people in town know our van.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it, and what's home life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I left school at sixteen and did farm work for a while, then Clive took me on four years ago. I've got my basic trade certificate, though I'm still slow on the roof work. I'm engaged to Hannah, who's a teaching assistant at the primary school, and we're getting married next summer at our chapel. We've got about three months of money saved, most of it meant for the wedding, and I don't use AI, never have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, told you. It's the same as every other fad from the cities. I wouldn't bother posting, I'd just say it down the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means life goes on, and that suits me. People always need roofs. I just want to get married, get good at the job and keep the van busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Learn the roofs properly, save for the wedding, and go to chapel on Sundays. Nothing would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, like it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be on your mind next year, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding, mainly, and the money for it. My fiancée Hannah and I want a deposit for a cottage by thirty, and the wedding eats most of what we've saved. That's a squeeze, but it's a good squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Clive run things? Has anything changed there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as he always has: a diary, a phone and a handshake. His daughter does the invoices on a laptop, and that's as much technology as Abbott Building gets.

say: I'd say AI was a **city fad** all along, like the others.
I'd say it **down the pub** with the lads, not online.
think: People will always **need roofs**, so life goes on.
I just want to **get married** and get good at the job.
do: Keep learning **roof work** from his uncle Clive.
S0.quote: My fiancée Hannah and I want a deposit for a cottage by thirty, and the wedding eats most of what we've saved.
fieldNote: Family firm and small-town work make him feel **secure**.
His money pressure is the **wedding** and a future deposit, not AI.
The firm runs on **handshakes**, with little technology.

steps.text: Keep learning roof work from his uncle Clive
Save for the wedding at the chapel next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck getting a robot up a barn roof in February. Folk round here wouldn't want it anyway. They want a man they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't think it touches me much. Maybe some fancy firms in the city get gadgets, but our customers are farmers and pensioners. They ring Clive because they know him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going like now. If anyone wants the paperwork done by computer, my cousin can handle that. I'd keep my head down and get good at roofs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a bit wary, but I don't see it on our jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Clive's daughter does the invoices on a laptop. What happens to that bit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the computer does it for her. Fine by me, she'd rather be on site anyway. Clive's daughter Rosie does the invoices on a laptop, and if a computer does them, Rosie just comes back on the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hannah works at a school. Does this touch her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the marking and the reports, I don't know. She's with the little ones, reading with them, wiping noses. I can't see a computer doing that, and I don't think parents would stand for it.

say: I'd say good luck getting a **robot** up a **barn roof** in February.
Customers round here want **a man they know**.
think: Our customers are **farmers and pensioners** who ring Clive directly.
Gadgets might reach **city firms**, but not our jobs.
do: Keep working as now and **get good at roofs** over the winter.
Leave any computer **paperwork** to his cousin Rosie at the firm.
feel: He feels **calm**, maybe a little wary.
S1.quote: Clive's daughter Rosie does the invoices on a laptop, and if a computer does them, Rosie just comes back on the tools.
fieldNote: He trusts **local relationships** to shield the firm.
He sees AI touching only the **invoicing**, done by a cousin.
He doesn't think **Hannah's school job** is exposed much.

steps.text: Keep working on roofs and getting faster up the ladder
Leave any new paperwork software to his cousin Rosie

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we shouldn't let it happen like that. Firms and families should look after their own, not wait for the government. I'd say that at chapel and in the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, I don't fully believe it. But if it's true, the big firms get robots that can do roofs by 2031, and they'd undercut Clive on price. Then the work dries up and the junior goes first, which is me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still get married, but small, and put the rest into savings. I'd ask Clive to teach me the skilled stuff faster, like lead work and repairs on old houses. I'd wait to see whether the robots really turn up before doing anything drastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit sick. Like a cold wind coming off the hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be thirty-one or so when the robots come. How does that land with the wedding and a cottage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd make me want a small wedding and a big savings pot. I'd rather marry Hannah (his fiancée) in the chapel hall with sandwiches than spend the cottage money on a fancy do. Then we'd see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if work dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. Clive, my parents, Hannah's parents. Chapel would rally round too. I'd not want benefits, but I'd take help from people who know me.

say: I'd say **families and firms** should look after their own.
I'd say that **at chapel** and in the pub.
think: I **don't fully believe** it would happen.
If it did, big firms with robots would **undercut Clive** by 2031.
do: Hold a **small wedding** and save the rest.
Ask Clive to teach **lead work** and old-house repairs faster.
**Wait and see** if robots really turn up.
feel: He feels **on edge** and a bit sick, like a cold wind coming.
S2.quote: I'd rather marry Hannah (his fiancée) in the chapel hall with sandwiches than spend the cottage money on a fancy do.
fieldNote: His doubt is **part disbelief**, part fear of being undercut.
He shrinks the **wedding** rather than the future savings.
He'd turn to **family and chapel**, not the state.

steps.text: Hold a small chapel hall wedding and bank the difference
Ask Clive to teach lead work and old-house repairs faster
Wait to see if roofing robots really appear locally

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so no need to panic. I'd say small firms like ours have survived worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'm a proper roofer by the time any robots turn up in 2034. But I'm still worried the big firms undercut us. And Clive's getting older, so I don't know if the firm will even be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and learn as much as I can. I'd save for the cottage as planned, maybe a bit slower. I'd stay with Clive and not try any new-fangled stuff until it was proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not like the fast one. It's out there on the horizon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years change the wedding or the cottage plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Wedding next summer, cottage by thirty, maybe a baby. I'm not going to put off a family because a computer might learn to fix a roof in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Clive ever buy one of these machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Clive. He'd sooner retire. Maybe Rosie would, if she took over. But Clive's a pen and paper man to his bones.

I'd say **small firms** like ours have survived worse.

Big firms could still **undercut us**, and Clive is ageing.
do: Keep learning with Clive and **stay with the firm**.
Save for the **cottage** as planned, a bit slower.
feel: He feels **worried**, but with the threat on the horizon.
S3.quote: I'm not going to put off a family because a computer might learn to fix a roof in 2034.
fieldNote: He refuses to change **family plans** for a possible future.
His worry ties to **Clive's age** as much as robots.
He won't try new tools until they're **proven**.

steps.text: Stay with Clive's firm and learn roofing fully
Save for the cottage deposit a bit more slowly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we'll manage. I'd tell the young lads to learn a proper trade and work hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm an experienced roofer by then. If the firm's still going, maybe I'm running it. I'd still be wary of the robots, but there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now for the first year. Wedding, save, learn. In a few years, talk to Clive about taking over part of the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. But mostly fine. It's far enough off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Clive's about sixty now. By 2036, who runs the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe me, if Clive trusts me with it. Running Abbott Building (his uncle's firm) at thirty-seven would make my granddad proud, robots or no robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about this, if you have them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade, work hard, look after your family. Same as I was told. I wouldn't tell them about robots till they were older.

I'd tell young lads to learn **a proper trade**.
think: I'd be an **experienced roofer** by 2036, with years behind me.
I might be **running the firm** if it's still going by then.

feel: He feels **mostly fine**, with a little unease.
S4.quote: Running Abbott Building (his uncle's firm) at thirty-seven would make my granddad proud, robots or no robots.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him dream of **running the family firm**.
Advice to future children stays **traditional**: trade, work, family.
He still carries a low **wariness** about robots.

steps.text: Keep saving for the cottage deposit after the wedding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. If the big firms get roofing robots by 2031, they'd undercut Clive and I'd be out. A cheaper roof from a big firm's robot could finish off a small builder that's served this town for forty years. What would help is apprenticeships and help for small family firms, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about faith. Whatever happens with jobs, we'll still have chapel and each other. That counts for more than people think.

He'd lean on **family and chapel**, not government, if work dried up.
His fear peaks with **AGI by 2028**, when big firms might undercut his uncle.
